Support vision and eye health every day
My mother was on eye injections for 8 years. The treatment didn't save her vision. I refused to follow that path.
And by the end of this, you're gonna be pissed.
Because there are three things happening right now:
One — Your blurry vision is giving you a countdown to injections or blindness that you don't want
Two — The medical system is pushing you toward treatments for life instead of fixing the root cause
And three — There's a multi-billion-dollar pharmaceutical industry that profits every single day you stay on expensive eye injections
So let me tell you what happened with my mother, because her story is gonna open your eyes to how messed up this really is.
For 8 YEARS, and I mean almost a decade straight, my mother was trapped on eye injection treatments.
Started with Eylea. Her retina specialist said it was "the gold standard" for wet macular degeneration. Said she'd need them regularly but they were "safe and effective."
Within six months, the anxiety started.
Not like normal worry. I'm talking that constant, gnawing dread about the next appointment. About having a needle put directly into her eyeball. About sitting in that waiting room knowing what was coming.
Her independence? Completely gone. She couldn't drive herself to appointments anymore. Had to rely on me or my sister for everything. Woman used to travel the world. Now she couldn't even get to the grocery store alone.
The vision loss got so bad she fell twice. Once on the stairs because she couldn't see the edge of the step. Another time in a parking lot because she didn't see the curb. My dad found her on the ground, crying.
And you know what the doctors said when we told them the injections weren't really helping?
"That's normal. Some patients stabilize, they don't improve."
"We can try a different medication if this one stops working."
"The injections are preventing it from getting worse faster."
So they switched her to Lucentis.
The anxiety stayed. Of course it did.
And you know what else?
Her vision got WORSE. Not better. Worse.
She went from reading large print books to needing a machine that magnified everything 10 times. Couldn't recognize faces across the room anymore. Stopped watching TV because she couldn't see it clearly.
My dad said it was like watching the woman he married slowly disappear into darkness.
And here's the part that made me sick to my stomach years later when I figured this out.
They had her on those injections for EIGHT YEARS.
Eight years of needles in her eyes. Eight years of watching her vision decline anyway. Eight years of doctor appointments where they'd adjust the treatment or switch the medication but never once, not ONE TIME, did anyone say "Hey, maybe we should look at what's CAUSING your macular degeneration instead of just treating the symptoms forever."
So fast forward to two years ago.
I'm 58 years old. I go to my annual eye exam. Doctor dilates my eyes and looks inside.
She frowns. Looks again.
And she says those words I'd been dreading my entire adult life:
"I'm seeing some early changes in your macula. Drusen deposits. It's the beginning of macular degeneration. We'll need to monitor this closely."
I felt my chest tighten.
Because I knew EXACTLY what that meant.
I'd watched my mother suffer for 8 years. The constant injections. The anxiety. The vision loss that kept progressing anyway. The complete loss of independence where she couldn't drive, couldn't read, couldn't see the faces of her grandchildren.
And I made a decision right there in that doctor's office.
I am NOT going on injections for the rest of my life.
I'm not following my mother's path.
There has to be another way.
So I did what they told me to do, right?
I started eating more leafy greens. Bought blue light blocking glasses. Started wearing sunglasses religiously outside.
Six months later, I go back for my follow-up appointment.
The drusen? Still there. Maybe slightly worse.
My doctor pulls out her referral pad.
"I think it's time we get you in to see a retina specialist. We need to monitor this more closely. If it progresses to wet AMD, we'll need to start injections immediately."
I looked at that referral and I felt rage building in my chest.
Because I'd DONE everything she told me to do. Everything the medical establishment says you're supposed to do. And it wasn't enough.
And now the only solution they have is the exact same injection protocol that failed to save my mother's vision for 8 years?
So at this point, I'm furious.
And I started asking questions that nobody wants you to ask.
Why are doctors so quick to "monitor" a condition that's actively destroying your vision but never fix the root cause?

My mind cannot be present for what is happening to me. She finally gets off me and I fall to the floor. She tears the back of my shirt open and strikes with her claws on my back as if to mark me as her property. I lay on the floor of the supply room crying. "Get up, Talia, " Sylvie  commands in my mind. “I said get up," she repeats. Her voice is stern but caring, "You're better than this. You will survive this." "I want to leave the world,  Sylvie . I can't do this anymore. I can't." "You can and you will. You will find your mate soon enough and things will change. I promise." "How can you be so sure?" "You will see. Glowy, burning hands are not your only gift." I get up, find an old cardigan in the back of the stockroom, and put it on. I go back to my room to find new clothes before making dinner. The next four days go without incident. Unless you consider I have gone to the roof several times contemplating my existence. Each time, I stand with my toes at the edge and stare down from the four-story building. I can't bring myself to do anything except cry and go back to my room. I can't do it to  Sylvie . I can't take her life because I want to take mine. Sunday after dinner service, I see Marcy in the hallway while I'm refilling pantries. She quickly approaches me and grabs me by the arm. She extends her claws into my bicep, drawing blood. "Talia, if you tell anyone and I mean anyone what you saw in George's office, I will make you suffer again," she says in a low threatening tone. Not again! I'm fed up. Does she want to bully me? Okay, fine. I lift my hat and let my violet eyes look directly at her. She gasps at the unusual sight. "Marcy, it would be a relief and I would welcome it. You don't care how I'm treated by this pack. Including you, your father, your mother, and your lover, too," Tears choke up in my throat. I cannot take any more punishment or threats from anyone else. I'm at my wit's end. If she takes my life right here in this hallway, it would be a relief. "I'm sorry,  Sylvie. I just can't do it anymore," I say to my angel as I'm staring down Marcy. She doesn't respond, she shuts our mind link and crawls into the corner of my mind. Marcy pushes me away, "Insolent bastard! You should be grateful for your life! The Alpha will hear about this." "I'm not grateful for this life, Marcy. And if you think I should be, you are part of the problem. If you want to tell the Alpha about this incident, I'm more than happy to tell him what instigated it." She stares at me with pure anger and hatred before walking away without a word. I guess fate has other plans for me. I stand in the hall for a few minutes to see if she is coming back, but she doesn't. I'm certain she is going to sabotage me. Maybe she's going to smother me in my sleep or just stab me straight in the back. Either way, I was serious when I told her I welcome her. I finish pantry duty making sure everything is set in the guest rooms. I had George order bouquets for each of the suites as an extra touch. In the guest Alpha's suite, I also added a bottle of champagne. If this is the last thing I ever get to do, I want it to be something that makes someone else happy. It is almost one-thirty in the morning before I plop into my bed totally exhausted. It has been a day. If Marcy has anything to do with it, it will probably be my last. Sylvie  is exhausted too. She stops sulking long enough to tell me she needs me to shift, but I can't. I have no time or energy. I keep promising her I will, but I feel like I've broken that promise. I float off to the sounds of her whimpering in my head while I cry into the pillow. To my surprise, my alarm wakes me in the morning. Sylvie  makes me promise to hang on for one more day. We go through the motions of the life I hate. While I'm getting ready, I look in the mirror to find my hair is completely silvery now. I tuck it into a bun to try to avoid people noticing it. The delegation from Dark Howlers arrives in the early afternoon. They are all tall and intimidating with tattoos and big muscles. Some of them have visible scars on their arms and faces. They're wearing matching business clothes or security uniforms. Luna Layla directs them to the sitting room while I quietly bring in pitchers of water and ice tea for them to drink. I do my best to try not to be noticed when one of the women calls me out. "You there, omega," She says abruptly. I look around and realize she is speaking to me. " For everyone." "Maya, of course, right away," Luna Layla says quickly, then nods her head to me. I rush to the cellar and pull out two cases of napkins, and glasses, prepping the drink service cart and head back to the sitting room. I open three bottles, leaving the rest for them to do as they wish and I back out of the room so I can start preparing dinner. The rest of the day goes without a hitch. The guests seem pleased with dinner. In the evening, I go to each guest suite to make sure everyone is happy with their accommodations. A couple of people ask for more bags of chips or soda but on the whole, everyone seems satisfied. The last door is the Beta's room. Maya opens the door, looking much more relaxed than earlier. She has a large tattoo of a rose and a dagger on her forearm. Her dark hair is still pulled back but she isn't wearing makeup. I can see now, she looks only a few years older than me. I can hear her mate inside talking on the phone. "Thanks for checking on us. Everything is wonderful. The flowers are a beautiful touch. You have good taste," she smiles at me. I bow to her slightly, then turn to leave. "Wait, what's under your hat?" I stop in my tracks and turn around. "I'm sorry ma'am?" I ask. I feel the blood drain from my face. "Your hat. Why is it so low? What are you trying to hide?" she asks, "Come closer." I come closer and slowly take off my hat. Keeping my eyes to the ground. My silver hair cascades down my back. It is embarrassingly greasy and visibly dirty. I feel myself blush. "Oh, I see," she says with surprise in her voice, "Now. Don't be disrespectful. Always look me in the eye when I speak to you." I look up at her. The light from her room shines right into my eyes. She looks at me blankly for a moment trying to process what she is seeing. "What are you? A hybrid?" "No, ma'am. The pack doctor did tests but doesn't know why it happened. He thinks it must be a transformation related to my wolf getting ready to wake up," I mean, it's not a lie...it's just not the whole truth, right? How am I supposed to tell a stranger that my wolf says I am the Moon Goddess's actual daughter and that is why I have silver hair and violet eyes? She grabs my chin and pulls my face closer to hers, inspecting closely, "And does the pack doctor know someone has broken your nose recently? You still have bruises." "He's treated my injuries in the past," I'm not trying to elaborate or implicate anyone to this person I don’t know. "Who's at the door, Maya?" the Beta inside calls to her. "Just the omega assigned to us, Caden. What's your name, again?" "It's Talia, ma'am but please call me Talia. I'm not an omega, though. I'm just a servant." "Her name is Talia. She picked out my beautiful flowers," she's still talking to her mate but she hasn't taken her eyes off me as if she is trying to size me up for some reason. Her brow furrows slightly as she stares. She's making me self-conscious. "That's nice. Ask her if I can get bubbly water in the refrigerator." "No problem, ma'am," She and I share a smile at 'bubbly water', "I will bring it shortly and leave it at the door.” "Thank you. Oh and Talia, if those bruises aren't healed tomorrow morning, find some powder. Alpha Damon does not tolerate seeing injuries like that." "Ye-yes, ma'am." I run to the stockroom, get four bottles of San Pellegrino, and put them in front of the door, then run away as fast as I can. One million questions run through my head. Would their Alpha be angry for being weaker than other wolves even if I was not part of his pack? Was she going to tell Alpha Edward about my unusual features? Was she going to call him out for letting someone break my nose? I mean, lady, if you think that is bad, I got some news you're not gonna like and then I'm dead meat by your Alpha for sure. Alpha Edward comes down later and whips me for not having all the items our guests wanted. By morning, Sylvie has still not been able to fully heal me. I’m in so much pain, everything is a struggle. Cooking, carrying breakfast trays, leaning over to clean tables. Every move causes scabs to open and bleed, making the back of my shirt damp with blood. Maya makes eye contact with me a couple of times. She can tell something was wrong but doesn't say anything. For some reason she can't explain, Sylvie is bouncing around in my head all morning. “The Beta is so nice! I can't wait to meet the Alpha and Luna!” “Sylvie , come on. We're not going to get to meet the Alpha and Luna. We're going to melt into the wallpaper and pretend we don't exist.” “I want to meet them.” “Okay, well I hate to disappoint you, but you're gonna get disappointed.” Layla comes in while I'm prepping lunch to let me know the Alpha has arrived and I need to make lunch for him as well. There is no Luna. He doesn't have a mate? And according to Layla...he's handsome. Not that it matters to me, because I'm going to be wallpaper. I don't want him to notice me at all. I take the trays to the conference room. Alpha Damon is not there but there is a spot at the table where he is supposed to sit. I leave his meal at the empty seat. Everyone from the Dark Howlers Pack politely thanks me as I lay plates in front of them. Their manners betray their intimidating features. No one from the Red Moon pack says a word to me as I serve them. I collect the trays and walk out quietly. Layla lets me know she will clean the plates so I can focus on dinner and food for the party. I go to the kitchen but need a minute to collect myself before I get started on dinner. I go out the back door and stand on the stoop. In the distance, I don't recognize him, it must be the Alpha from Dark Howlers. He is too far away for me to see his actual features though. All I can see is a tall figure with dark hair and a suit. It smells like but I swear it smells like coffee too...or dark chocolate. This guy was a mocha drinker? I laugh to myself at the thought of the big bad Alpha of Dark Howlers sipping on a mochaccino. I make a four-course meal of Caesar salad, bacon-wrapped shrimp appetizers, beef wellington with braised Brussels sprouts for the main dish, and a key lime pie for dessert. I also make bruschetta, tomato fritters, mini calzones, assorted veggie trays with dip, and chocolate truffles to serve for the party. I finished the desserts and veggie trays between breakfast and lunch so there was less for me to worry about now. I realize Sylvie 's advice of finding happiness in cooking has helped me enjoy making this dinner. Maybe because I'm serving people other than my pack or maybe it's because I'm making special food, not just the regular stuff I make for the pack? Either way, I don't mind my work today. I felt a sense of pride in it. There are servers for dinner service since it's a formal event. I stay in the kitchen and make sure everything is plated and going out the door in perfect condition. I'm in the zone, as they say. I peek out from the kitchen after each course is served. People seem to enjoy the food, which is a relief. I notice Alpha Edward is getting pretty drunk. Luna Layla keeps taking his glass away from him, but he keeps ordering the omegas to give him more. The dining room is extra crowded, so I don't get a better look at Alpha Damon. Maya sees me peeking out from the kitchen and gives me a wink and thumbs up. I smile and give a little wave before pulling my head back. I help the servers take the party food to the tables at the edges of the ballroom. I also make sure the bars in the corners are fully stocked. The DJ is finishing setting up and colorful lights are sliding across the floor. Party balloons and streamers are hanging all over the place. The first few guests are starting to wander in which is my cue to duck out the back door. Luckily, the dinner servers will clean up the dinner service tonight, which gives me extra time to restock pantries. I head upstairs to the stockroom and load the cart up. I'm humming to myself as I go from room to room. I feel an odd sense of calm as I go. "You're in a good mood," Sylvie  says. "I guess. I'm not sure why though. My back and feet still make me feel bad. " "Well, I'm happy that you're happy for once. This version of you is pretty cool." "Thanks,  Sylvie . You're not half bad yourself." I finish stocking the ranked pack members' rooms on the fourth and third floors. Then head to the second floor where the guest suites are. The cleaning staff has cleaned the rooms and bathrooms. I just need to restock the toiletries, pantry items, and refrigerators. I make quick work of the rooms. I remember to stock the Betas' room with more bottles of San Pellegrino, refresh the flowers, and leave a little tent card with a handwritten smiley face on the kitchenette counter. 

It was almost midnight by the time I was wrapping up, and everyone was still in the ballroom. 

I closed the door to the Beta's suite and moved on to the Alpha's suite door. 

It's the last room left. He must be at the party too, but I knocked before entering just in case.

I put my ear against the door and heard nothing, so I slipped my key in the lock and opened the door, but the moment I looked inside, my heart stopped, and I froze. 

Standing there was the most handsome werewolf I've ever seen in my life.

Easily six foot, six inches tall, looked to be about two hundred fifty pounds of solid muscle with the broadest shoulders, but he wasn’t alone, an icy Blonde stood in front of him with her hands undoing his belt.

The smell of coffee and dark chocolate filled the air, and my mind went hazy as I froze, seeing two piercing blue eyes staring back at me. 

"Stop!" He shouted.

'Is this it? Is this the day I die?' I wondered.

I was only doing my job, but that did not change the fact that I had witnessed something that should not have been seen.

Before I could move, he lunged forward and roughly pinned me against the floor outside the room with a low growl. 

He placed both hands on my shoulders, preventing me from escaping, put his face against my neck, and inhaled deeply. My heart was pounding in my chest as overwhelming panic began to set in.

“Alpha Damon, is this Omega trying to steal something?” A guard said, seeing the struggle. 

“Get back.” He snarled, flashing his large fangs.

“Mine,” he growled. 

Over his shoulder, I could faintly see Marcy staring daggers at me, and down the hall, I heard Alpha Edward shouting. 

‘What a disaster’ I thought, ‘they’re all going to kill me.’

My head started swimming, and I felt even dizzier, maybe I was finally dying. 

“Look what, you’ve done you little bitch!” 

Marcy yelled as she reached out to grab me, but she never touched me, Alpha Damon snarled, snatching her hand out of the air and snapping her wrist. 

Alpha Edward roared, “How dare you! This is war!”

I watched them fight as if it was a dream. They looked as though they were moving in slow motion. 

Alpha Edward yanked Marcy, pulling her back as Damon snarled at them, he was vicious, beautifully vicious.

A guard tried to separate them as Beta Caden and Maya took defensive positions around Alpha Damon, and George lunged at Damon, but he was no match for the Alpha.

Damon grabbed George by the throat and threw him into the wall as though her were a tiny pup.

I almost laughed, but I was shaking all over, barely able to stand, but in the chaos, I managed to crawl away and slink down the stairs. 

I looked around to see if anyone noticed me, but they were all too busy arguing.

I looked down to see blood running down my legs, dripping onto the floor. I started to lose consciousness, and then I heard it, the most guttural, ear-shattering roar.

“WHERE IS SHE?!”

“Where is who, Alpha Damon?”

“WHERE IS MY MATE?!”

Is it possible?
Is Talia truly Damon’s fated mate?
What will Damon do to protect her?
Will their bond ignite a war between the two most powerful packs in the order?
Will any of them leave Red Moon territory alive?

BOTOX® Cosmetic (onabotulinumtoxinA) is a prescription medicine that is injected into muscles and used to temporarily improve the look of moderate to severe forehead lines, crow's feet, and frown lines between the eyebrows in adults. 
-
Talk to your doctor about BOTOX® Cosmetic and whether it’s right for you. There are risks with this product—the effects of BOTOX® Cosmetic may spread hours to weeks after injection causing serious symptoms. Alert your doctor right away as difficulty swallowing, speaking, breathing, eye problems or muscle weakness can be a sign of a life-threatening condition. If this happens, do not drive a car, operate machinery, or do other dangerous activities. Patients with these conditions before injection are at the highest risk. Swallowing problems may last for several months. Side effects may include allergic reactions, neck and injection-site pain, fatigue and headache. Don’t receive BOTOX® Cosmetic if there’s a skin infection. Tell your doctor your medical history, muscle or nerve conditions, and medications, including botulinum toxins, as these may increase the risk of serious side effects.

I used to rewrite emails seven times before hitting send. You know that feeling, right? When you've crafted the "perfect" response, but then you read it again and suddenly it sounds too casual. That's exactly why this interactive bracelet has become my daily reality check. The moment I catch myself spiraling into that familiar "it's not good enough" loop, I tap my phone to my wrist. Instantly, an affirmation appears that meets me right in that perfectionist panic.

Sometimes it's "Done is better than perfect." Other times it might be "Your worth isn't measured by your mistakes." The app somehow knows exactly what I need to hear when my inner perfectionist starts running the show.

It's like having a wise friend right there with you, ready to remind you that progress beats perfection every single time. Someone who remembers that the goal isn't to be flawless - it's to keep moving forward, even when forward feels messy.

Because here's what perfectionism doesn't want you to know: every single thing you admire was created by someone who decided that "good enough to share" was better than "perfect but hidden." Every book, every song, every piece of art that's ever moved you - none of it was perfect. But all of it was brave enough to exist.

If you've been stuck in the perfectionist trap lately, maybe it's time to give yourself permission to be beautifully, imperfectly human.

Numbing pain. Masking it.

And if you’ve been stuck in a cycle of pain, pills, and appointments…

If you’ve been told it’s “normal”…

I want you to know: that’s NOT the whole story.

You haven’t failed.

Why everyone fatigued should be grounding
I'm going to sound crazy, but hear me out.

(Anyone struggling with fatigue or low energy, this is for you.)

Until 2 weeks ago, I was waking up exhausted EVERY morning. Didn't matter if I slept 4 hours or 8 hours, I'd wake up feeling like I didn’t sleep at all. By noon I'd already be drained, brain fog so bad I couldn’t focus on anything. Couldn't remember the last time I felt like myself. I felt tired and annoyed all the time.

I'd tried everything. Blackout curtains. Supplement after supplement. From drinking 5 coffees a day just to function to quitting coffee completely to see if that would help. I even tried going on a gluten-free diet. But basically nothing I tried did anything. 

Then I saw this article pop up on Facebook written by a rheumatologist from New York. I almost scrolled past it but the headline was something about fatigue not just being about sleep and I was like... Wait what?

Read the whole thing. He was talking about how there's this deeper issue people don't talk enough about that makes the symptoms so much worse. He mentioned grounding therapy and that these grounding sheets can be helpful to bring back energy levels naturally.

(I don't remember the exact details, if you're curious just read the article I've linked below.)

Anyways, I was obviously skeptical. But at that point I'd already wasted money on everything else that didn't work, and this had a 90-day money-back guarantee so I figured why not. They seemed confident, and there was literally nothing to lose because I would just return it if it didn't work.

Got the sheet, plugged it in, went to sleep thinking "this is ridiculous." I even laughed at myself for even trying something like this.

But the next morning as I was brushing my teeth, I realized that I’d slept through the ENTIRE night - for NINE HOURS. And for the first time in I don't even know how long, I wasn't thinking about being tired and what I should do to not feel tired. If you struggle with fatigue, you know exactly what I’m talking about.

The next morning I woke up and actually felt... refreshed? My husband looked at me like "How long have you been awake?" because apparently I didn’t look as tired. But I only woke up a couple of minutes before him.

Two weeks in - I feel 10 years younger. The midday crashes are basically gone. I only have one cup of coffee in the morning, and I still sleep better than I have in years. Brain fog seems to have gone down too. I can’t describe it but my mind feels more clear.

And I haven't bitten anyone's head off in a while (my husband loves it too).

I know this might sound crazy but I figured if it helped me, maybe it can also help other ladies out there going through this nightmare of feeling tired 24/7.

My CO Detector Almost Killed My Family
I've been a firefighter for 7 years. Nine months ago, I went home at 4 AM and ripped every detector off my own walls.

I thought I'd seen everything.

House fires. Car accidents. Medical emergencies. All of it.

But nothing prepared me for the call we got at 1:47 AM on a Tuesday in May.

"Family of four. Possible carbon monoxide. Ambulance en route."

We pulled up to a quiet suburban street. Lights on in the house. Front door wide open.

A man was standing on the lawn in his pajamas. Two kids sitting on the grass wrapped in blankets. A woman on her knees throwing up.

Neighbor was with them. She's the one who called 911.

"I couldn't sleep," she said. "Saw them stumble outside. Something's very wrong."

I grabbed my meter and went inside.

The reading hit me before I even made it to the hallway.

48 PPM in the living room. 67 PPM near the bedrooms. Over 90 PPM in the basement.

This family had been breathing poison all night.

I walked back outside.

The paramedics were putting oxygen masks on the kids. The mom was still dry heaving. The dad looked pale, disoriented.

"How long were you inside?" I asked him.

"We went to bed around 10," he said. His words were slurred. "Woke up maybe 20 minutes ago. Something felt wrong."

"You got lucky," I said. "Another hour and we'd be having a very different conversation."

I went back inside to find the source.

Furnace in the basement. Heat exchanger had a crack you could barely see. Every time it fired up, carbon monoxide leaked into the ductwork and spread through the whole house.

Classic case.

But here's what got me.

As I was walking through the hallway, I saw it.

A carbon monoxide detector. Plugged into the wall outlet.

Little green light glowing.

I checked my meter again. 67 PPM right where I was standing.

The detector was silent.

I pulled it off the wall and brought it outside.

The dad saw me holding it.

"That's supposed to keep us safe," he said. "Why didn't it go off?"

I turned it over and checked the back.

First Alert. Manufactured in 2024.

"When did you buy this?" I asked.

"Six months ago," he said. "Right after we moved in. Got it at Lowe's."

"You test it?"

"Every month. It always beeps. The green light's always on."

His wife looked at me.

"I thought these things lasted seven years?"

"They do," I said. "But that's not the problem."

I showed them the reading on my meter.

"This detector is brand new. It's working perfectly. The sensor is fine. The battery is fine. The speaker works."

"Then why didn't it go off?" the dad asked.

"Because it's designed to wait until you hit 70 parts per million before it alarms."

They stared at me.

"Your levels were at 67. Right below the threshold. It was doing exactly what it's supposed to do."

"But we were dying," the mom said.

"I know."

I looked at the two kids wrapped in blankets. The boy couldn't have been more than eight. The girl looked about five.

"At 70 PPM, you've already been breathing poison for hours. You're already symptomatic. Headache. Nausea. Confusion. Your kids have been sleeping in it all night."

I paused.

"And that's if it's rising slow. If you've got a serious leak and levels jump fast, by the time this thing decides to beep, there's a very good chance you're already too sick, too confused, too weak to respond."

The dad just stared at the detector in my hand.

"But we did everything right," he said. "We bought a detector. We tested it. We thought we were safe."

"You're not the first family to think that," I said. "And you won't be the last."

The ambulance took them to the hospital. Oxygen therapy. Observation. They got lucky.

I went home that night around 4 AM.

My wife was asleep. My two daughters were in their rooms.

I walked into the hallway and looked at our detector.

Same brand. Same model. Same little green light glowing.

I'd tested it two weeks ago. It beeped loud. Green light came back on.

I thought that meant it worked.

I grabbed my work meter from my truck and walked through the house.

0 PPM everywhere. We were fine.

But I realized something that made my stomach turn.

If we ever DID have a leak, this detector wouldn't warn us until it was almost too late.

Just like that family.

I sat down at my kitchen table and started researching.

Those cheap detectors — the ones at Home Depot, Lowe's, Walmart, the ones in 90% of American homes — they're designed to meet minimum UL safety standards.

Not to actually save your life.

The UL standard requires them to alarm at 70 PPM within 60 to 240 minutes.

70 PPM. And they can take up to FOUR HOURS to make a sound.

And they're ALLOWED to stay completely silent at lower levels. 30 PPM? 40 PPM? 50 PPM? Levels that are absolutely dangerous, especially for kids and elderly people?

The detector doesn't have to do anything.

It's not broken. It's not defective. It's working exactly as designed.

And that design is killing people.

I went back to the station the next day and told the other guys.

One of the veterans, Martinez, pulled me aside.

"You remember that call three months ago? The family on Maple Street?"

I nodded. I'd been there.

Mom, dad, three kids. We found them in the morning. Neighbor called it in when the kids didn't show up for the school bus.

All five of them gone.

CO poisoning from a cracked heat exchanger.

"They had detectors," Martinez said. "Brand new. The levels built slowly all night. By the time they hit 70 PPM, the family was already too far gone. Too asleep. Too poisoned."

He paused.

"After that call, I was losing my mind. My brother-in-law's an HVAC tech. Been doing it for 20 years. I called him and asked what he uses in his own house."

He showed me his phone.

"Steadfast Haven. Said it's what all the HVAC guys use because they see furnace failures every single day. They know what the cheap ones miss."

It wasn't just a detector with a light. It had a digital display. Real-time PPM readings for both CO and natural gas.

"Alarms at 10 PPM," Martinez said. "Dual sensors. My brother-in-law said he wouldn't let his family sleep in a house without one."

That night, I ordered a 4-pack.

One for each floor. One near the furnace. One in the kitchen by the gas stove.

I pulled every old detector off the walls. Threw them in the trash.

Plugged in the new ones and watched the displays light up.

0 PPM CO. 0 PPM gas. Temperature reading. Humidity.

Real information. Not just a meaningless green light.

For the first time in my career, I actually felt like my family was protected.

Not because I hoped it would work.

Because I could see proof.

That was nine months ago.

And I haven't shut up about it since.

The "Weird Sheet" In Our 5-Star Airbnb
I run an Airbnb. The other day, I got a text from my guest that made me cry.

"I'm not joking, I woke up and cried. I forgot what it felt like to actually rest. Please share with me where you got those. Because I need one for every bed in my house."

Let me back up.

So my husband and I have been running a five-star Airbnb for the past 4 years. 

And about 6 months ago, something weird started happening.

Guests would check out and leave reviews like:

“Got the best sleep of my entire life here.”
“Best spot ever, slept through the entire night for all 3 nights. That never happens."
“Seriously need to know what sheets those are.”

At first, I thought it was just the “vacation effect”. People are relaxed, they're unplugged, they're happy.

But then a guest named Susan, a woman in her 50s, pulled me aside before checkout.

She looked me dead in the eyes and said: "I need to know what's on that bed. I have fibromyalgia. I haven't slept through the night in 8 years. But last few nights I did."

I told her about the grounding sheets.

She stared at me. "The what?"

I explained the whole thing to her. How they connect you to the Earth's electrical charge while you sleep. How the silver fibers conduct electrons that bring down inflammation.

She ordered one before she even left.

Two weeks later, she sent me a photo of her bedroom. She'd put grounding sheets on every single bed in her house.

That's when I realized: this isn't just an Airbnb thing. This is real.

So let me tell you what these sheets actually do, because I didn't believe it at first either.

Most people don't realize this, but your body builds up a positive electrical charge throughout the day. You're surrounded by Wi-Fi, electronics, phones, screens—all of it creates what's called "dirty electricity."

Your body stores it. And that stored charge? It drives inflammation.
Which leads to pain.
Which leads to restless, broken sleep where you wake up feeling worse than when you went to bed.

Grounding sheets REVERSE that.

The silver fibers woven into the fabric act like a conductor. You plug the cord into the grounding port in your wall—the third hole in the outlet that's connected to the Earth outside—and while you sleep, electrons flow from the ground into your body.

Those electrons neutralize the inflammation. Your nervous system calms down. Your cortisol drops. Your body finally gets into deep, restorative sleep.

And when you wake up? Your back doesn't hurt. Your neck isn't stiff. You don't feel like you got hit by a truck.

You just feel... rested.

I bought my first GroundingWell sheet three years ago because I kept hearing about grounding from a friend who wouldn't shut up about it.

I didn't think it would work. I thought it was pseudoscience.

But the first morning I woke up after using it, I sat up in bed and literally looked around the room like something was wrong.

My shoulders that were chronically tight for years felt relaxed.

My husband noticed immediately. "You didn't toss and turn last night. Not even once."

Within two weeks, the neck pain I'd had since my 30s was gone.

I wasn't expecting that. I just wanted to sleep better.

That's when I bought sheets for the Airbnb. All four beds. And then our guest room at home. And then my mom's house because she kept complaining about her joints.

We probably own seven or eight of these sheets now.

And the guest reviews? They changed completely.

Before the grounding sheets, we'd get: "Great location, clean, comfortable."

After? "I've never slept better in my life. I'm buying whatever sheets these are."

We've had guests rebook specifically to sleep in our beds again. We've had guests ask if they can buy the sheets off us. One couple extended their stay by two nights because the husband's sciatica, which he'd dealt with for 15 years—got so much better he didn't want to leave.

That's not the mattress. That's not the pillows. That's the grounding sheets.

Here's what I wish someone had told me three years ago:

Not all grounding sheets work. MOST of them are garbage.

We’ve tried 5 other brands, but GroundingWell is the one we keep coming back to. Their sheets use pure silver fiber woven throughout the entire fabric—not just a coating that washes off after three uses like the cheap Amazon knockoffs.

BOTOX® Cosmetic (onabotulinumtoxinA) is a prescription medicine that is injected into muscles and used to temporarily improve the look of moderate to severe forehead lines, crow's feet, and frown lines between the eyebrows in adults.
-
Talk to your doctor about BOTOX® Cosmetic and whether it’s right for you. There are risks with this product—the effects of BOTOX® Cosmetic may spread hours to weeks after injection causing serious symptoms. Alert your doctor right away as difficulty swallowing, speaking, breathing, eye problems or muscle weakness can be a sign of a life-threatening condition. If this happens, do not drive a car, operate machinery, or do other dangerous activities. Patients with these conditions before injection are at the highest risk. Swallowing problems may last for several months. Side effects may include allergic reactions, neck and injection-site pain, fatigue and headache. Allergic reactions can include rash, welts, asthma symptoms, and dizziness. Don’t receive BOTOX® Cosmetic if there’s a skin infection. Tell your doctor your medical history, muscle or nerve conditions (including ALS/Lou Gehrig's disease, myasthenia gravis, or Lambert-Eaton syndrome), and medications, including botulinum toxins, as these may increase the risk of serious side effects.

When preparing for a Temporary Duty (TDY) assignment, selecting the right lodging is a crucial decision that can significantly impact your overall experience. While hotels have long been the standard choice, short-term rentals (STRs) are increasingly becoming the preferred option for military personnel. STRs offer numerous benefits, from enhanced privacy to cost savings, but understanding the process to secure one can be the key to making this transition seamless. Here’s a step-by-step guide to help you navigate the process of choosing a short-term rental over a hotel for your next TDY assignment.

Step 1: Submit an Initial Request for Reservation
The process begins with submitting an initial request for your TDY lodging. At 9 Line Agency, we make this step as straightforward as possible. You’ll need to provide essential details, including the number of people traveling, the duration of the stay, and the desired location. This information allows us to tailor our offerings to your specific needs, ensuring that we can find the perfect accommodations for your assignment.

Step 2: Pre-Emptive Planning and Exploring Options
Once we receive your request, our team at 9 Line Agency will engage in pre-emptive planning. We understand that the military’s needs can vary greatly, so we provide a range of options that showcase our capability to accommodate different group sizes and requirements. Whether you’re booking for one person or an entire unit, we’ll present you with multiple choices, each designed to support your mission effectively. This step is crucial in demonstrating how STRs can offer superior value compared to traditional hotels.

Step 3: Secure Final Approval from Your Unit
Before finalizing any lodging arrangements, it’s essential to obtain approval from your unit. This step ensures that your chosen accommodations align with military standards and mission requirements. At this stage, your unit will review the options provided and make a decision based on what best suits the operational needs. Having a variety of STR options available can make it easier to secure this approval, as they often provide more flexibility and comfort compared to standard hotel rooms. This step may include 9 Line Agency sharing the approved memos for your unit to approve prior to traveling, helping to get Non-A letters if applicable and much more depending on your unit's needs. 

Step 4: Reserve and Secure Your Short-Term Rental
Once your unit has approved the STR option, the next step is to reserve and secure the appropriate number of rentals to support the mission. At 9 Line Agency, we handle this process for you, ensuring that all details are confirmed well in advance. This includes securing multiple properties in close proximity if necessary, or setting up a “planning house” to serve as a central hub for your team. Our goal is to make sure that all logistics are taken care of so that you can focus on your mission.

Step 5: Receive Final Invoices and Prepare for Your Stay
Approximately 30 days before your scheduled arrival, we’ll send you the final invoices. This step allows for any necessary financial arrangements to be made well ahead of time, ensuring there are no surprises upon arrival. With everything confirmed, you can focus on preparing for your assignment, knowing that your lodging is secured and ready.

Step 6: Check-In and Enjoy a Smooth Stay
Finally, two days before your arrival, we’ll provide you with detailed check-in procedures. At 9 Line Agency, we understand the importance of a seamless experience, so we also monitor your trip to ensure everything goes as planned. Our team is on hand to address any issues that may arise, ensuring that your stay is as comfortable and efficient as possible.

Why Choose a Short-Term Rental (Nonconventional Lodging) Over a Hotel?

Opting for a short-term rental over a hotel offers numerous advantages for military personnel on TDY assignments. STRs provide enhanced privacy, with more space for planning and relaxation. They also feature fully equipped kitchens, promoting healthier living and camaraderie among your team. Additionally, STRs often result in significant cost savings, allowing you to stay within your per diem while enjoying a superior lodging experience.
By following this straightforward process, you can easily secure a short-term rental that not only meets but exceeds the standards of traditional hotel accommodations. At 9 Line Agency, we are dedicated to making your TDY experience as smooth and successful as possible, ensuring that your lodging supports your mission every step of the way.

Picture this: It's 2:47 AM when the first transformer explodes.

You're jolted awake by the sound — like thunder, but closer. Through your window, you see a flash of blue-white light on the horizon. Then another. And another.

Your phone's dead. You reach for it instinctively, press the power button. Nothing. You try the light switch. Nothing.

You walk to the window and look outside. Your entire neighborhood is dark. No streetlights. No porch lights glowing. Not a single house light anywhere. Even the intersection at the end of your street — the one that always has that annoying blinking yellow light — is completely black.

In the distance, you hear sirens. Lots of them. Then you hear something else. Car alarms. Dozens of them going off at once, then dying out one by one.

Your neighbor — the retired Army guy who never talks much — is already standing in his driveway in his bathrobe, staring at the sky. You throw on some clothes and walk outside.

"What's happening?" you ask him.

He doesn't look at you when he responds. His eyes are still fixed on the horizon. "Grid's down. This could be bad."

"Like a power outage?"

"No." He shakes his head slowly. "Power outages don't kill car electronics. This is different."

You walk back to your car and try to start it. Nothing. Not even a click. You pop the hood and stare at the engine like you know what you're looking at. You don't.

Your neighbor walks over. "EMP probably. Electromagnetic pulse. Fried everything with a circuit board." He points down the street. "See that old truck? The '89 Ford? That'll probably still run. No computer system. But everything else?" He gestures at your car. "Dead."

The sun starts coming up a few hours later, and that's when you really see it. Cars are stopped in the middle of the road. Some crashed into each other at intersections when the lights went out. You can hear people yelling in the distance. Someone's screaming.

You try your phone again. Still nothing. You try the landline. Dead. You turn on your battery-powered radio and scan through static until you find something. A crackling voice, barely audible:

"...if you can hear this... stay in your homes... emergency broadcast... do not attempt to travel... unknown duration..."

Then it cuts out.

By mid-morning, you see your neighbors starting to gather in the street. Everyone's confused. Scared. Someone says they heard an explosion at the substation. Someone else says it's a cyberattack. Another person swears they saw a flash in the sky before everything went dark.

Nobody knows anything for sure.

But everyone's starting to realize this isn't a normal power outage.

By day three, your local Walmart looks like a war zone.

The shelves are empty. Not just the water aisle — everything. The employees stopped showing up on day two when they realized they weren't getting paid and couldn't even drive to work. The people who are still there aren't shopping anymore.

They're taking.

You walked there because your car still won't start. It took you two hours. Your feet hurt. And when you finally get inside, you realize you're too late.

The bottled water section is completely ransacked. Not a single bottle left. Just empty shelves and torn cardboard. You see two guys screaming at each other over a case of Gatorade. One of them has a baseball bat.

You leave.

Now, you might be thinking this sounds like some Hollywood disaster movie scenario.

I used to think the same thing.

But here's what most people don't know: this has already happened. Multiple times.

In February 2021, the Texas power grid collapsed. Four million people without electricity for a week in the middle of winter. Frozen pipes. No heat. And here's the part nobody talks about — fourteen million people were under boil-water advisories because when the grid went down, so did the water treatment plants.

People had water coming out of their taps that was full of bacteria. Undrinkable.

In 2003, the Northeast Blackout hit 55 million people across eight states. Power went out for days. Water treatment systems failed. Pumping stations went offline.

In August 2020, California had rolling blackouts during a heatwave. Water systems struggled. Treatment plants ran on backup generators until the fuel ran out.

This isn't science fiction. This is recent history.

And every single time, the same pattern emerges. Within hours, bottled water completely sells out. Every store within 50 miles is cleared out. And the people who survived without major problems weren't the ones with the biggest stockpiles.

They were the ones who could make their own clean water.

Here's the thing nobody thinks about until it's too late:

If the power went out right now — not from an EMP, just from a normal grid failure or cyberattack — you'd probably be fine for a while.

Think about it. You've got food in your pantry right now. Canned soup. Pasta. Rice. Crackers. Random stuff that would keep you fed for at least a week, probably longer.

But water?

How much water do you actually have in your house at this exact moment? A couple bottles in the fridge? Maybe one of those cases from Costco that's been sitting in the garage for six months?

That's three days. Four if you're careful.

Your body can survive three weeks without food.

But without water? Just three days.

Not "three days of being thirsty." Three days until your organs start failing. Your brain stops working. Your body shuts down.

And here's what makes it worse — when the power goes out and stays out, your tap water becomes dangerous within 24-48 hours. The treatment plants run on backup generators, and once those run out of fuel, the water stops being treated.

It's still flowing. But it's not safe.

Let me show you what actually happens in the first 72 hours.

Hour 1-6: Most people don't even think about water yet. They're worried about their phones. Their internet. Whether the food in the fridge will spoil.

Hour 6-12: Reality sets in. If the power's been out this long, it's not coming back soon. People start heading to stores. The smart ones get there first.

Hour 12-24: Bottled water is completely gone. Not low stock — GONE. Empty shelves at every grocery store, gas station, convenience store within 50 miles. People start buying anything liquid. Soft drinks. Juice. Energy drinks.

Day 2: Those are gone too. People start getting creative. Some remember they have swimming pools and start drinking chlorinated water. They get sick. Others try to boil water on camping stoves, but fuel runs out fast.

Day 3: People start making desperate decisions. They drink from streams. Garden hoses. Rain puddles. Anywhere they can find water.

And that's when the real problems start.

Because every natural water source is contaminated.

E. coli from animal waste. Giardia from decomposing organic matter. Cryptosporidium from runoff. This stuff lives in virtually every creek, stream, pond, and lake.

During the Texas freeze, emergency rooms were flooded with people who drank untreated water. Violent dysentery. Vomiting. Severe dehydration on top of already being dehydrated.

It turned a survivable situation into a crisis.

So when the grid goes down, you're stuck between two bad options:

Die of dehydration in three days.

Or drink contaminated water and get so sick you wish you were dead.

Unless there's a third option.

Here's what I learned from talking to people who actually lived through the Texas freeze.

The families who came out okay weren't the ones with garages full of bottled water. That ran out just as fast as everyone else's.

They were the families who had a way to filter water. To turn pool water, rainwater, and snow melt into something safe to drink.

Not by boiling — that takes fuel, time, equipment, and it doesn't even remove everything. Just kills some bacteria.

These families had portable filters that could remove bacteria and parasites instantly. Small enough to fit in a drawer. No power needed. No batteries.

Just clean water, whenever they needed it.

And that's what got me thinking.

I'm not a prepper. I don't have a bunker. I don't stockpile stuff.

But after seeing what happened in Texas, and reading about the grid vulnerabilities, I started asking myself: if the power went out tomorrow and stayed out for a week, would my family be okay?

Food? Yeah, we'd be fine. We've got enough random stuff in the pantry.

But water? We'd be in serious trouble by day three.

So I started looking into solutions.

Not the cheap camping filters that break after 20 uses. Not the expensive whole-house systems that need installation and power.

I needed something simple. Something that works when nothing else does. Something that gives me unlimited clean water from any source.

That's when I found the HYDRA-X1.

This is what I keep in my house now. One in the kitchen drawer. One in each car. One in my work bag.

Here's why:

It uses 0.1-micron hollow-fiber membrane technology. Those holes are so microscopically small that bacteria and parasites physically cannot fit through. They get trapped. Clean water passes through.

It removes bacteria like E. coli, Salmonella, Cholera, and Typhoid. Parasites like Giardia and Cryptosporidium. All the stuff that'll put you in the hospital when you can't even get to a hospital.

Filters up to 400 gallons. That's over a year of drinking water for one person. Months for a family.

Weighs 2 ounces. Fits in your pocket. No shelf life — it works in 10 years the same as it works today.

Works three different ways depending on what you need. Sip directly from a water source. Screw it onto a water bottle. Attach the squeeze bag and let gravity do the work.

No power. No batteries. No complexity.

Just clean drinking water.

Here's what this actually means:

When the next grid failure happens — and based on what experts are saying, it's not if but when — you won't be fighting people at empty stores.

You won't be drinking chlorinated pool water and getting sick.

You won't be watching your kids go thirsty because you ran out of bottled water on day two.

You'll walk to the nearest creek, pond, or lake. You'll use rainwater. You'll use your neighbor's pool if it comes to that.

And you'll have unlimited clean water while everyone else is panicking.

That's the difference.

I'm not trying to scare you or sell you on some doomsday scenario.

I'm just telling you what I did after looking at what actually happens when the power grid goes down and realizing I wasn't ready for it.

The HYDRA-X1 is what I trust for my family. I've tested it. I've run it through some pretty sketchy water sources just to see if it works. It does.

It's the kind of thing you hope you never need. But if you do need it, you need it bad. And by then, it's too late to get one.

Why every menopausal woman should be grounding
"Are you seeing someone?" That's what my husband asked me last Tuesday. Dead serious.

I was so shocked. I just stared at him confused. 

"What? No. Why would you even…"

"Something’s up with you. You're different. You've been different for weeks. You're... happier all the sudden. So I thought maybe..."

I started crying. Not sad crying. Just... I didn't realize how bad things had gotten between us until he said that.

Let me back up.

I'm 52. For the past two years, menopause has been destroying me. And destroying my marriage.

The night sweats meant I was up at 2am every night, which meant he was up too. I'd have to change my pajamas, sometimes even put a towel down on the sheets. We were both exhausted.

The mood swings were worse. I'd snap at him over the tiniest things. He'd leave a cup on the counter and I'd lose it. Then I'd feel guilty and apologize, but the damage would already be done.

Slowly we started avoiding each other. Stopped talking. Stopped touching. We were just existing in the same house.

I'd tried everything. Expensive hormone creams. Supplements that did nothing. My doctor basically said "this is normal, you'll get over it."

I was adjusting to being miserable. And so was my husband.

Then about two months ago, I saw this article pop up on Facebook. It was written by a gynecologist from New York, and it was something about menopause not just being about hormones.

I almost scrolled past it. But I clicked.

She was talking about how there's this deeper issue that makes menopausal symptoms so much worse. 

She mentioned grounding therapy and how grounding sheets helped many of her patients.

(I don't remember all the exact details. If you want to read it, I've linked it below.)

It sounded absolutely insane. 

But at that point, I'd already wasted money on everything else. And this had a 90-day money-back guarantee.

I ordered the GroundingWell bedsheet without telling my husband. When it arrived, I opened the box in the bedroom.

He walked in and saw me laying out this long rectangular strip across our bed.

"What is that?"

"It's a grounding sheet. It goes on top our sheet and it—"

"How much did you spend?"

I told him.

He just closed his eyes and sighed. "Another thing that won't work. Great."

"They have a 90-day guarantee."

"We both know you're not going to actually return it."

I stayed silent.

“I’ll just put it on my side of the bed, then.”

I laid the sheet and plugged the cord into the outlet. My husband just shook his head and got into bed on his side, as far away from it as possible.

First night, I slept through without waking up drenched. I thought it was a fluke.

But it happened again the next night. And the night after that.

By the end of the first week, I realized I'd slept through the entire night seven days in a row. For the first time in 3 years, by the way.

I didn't say anything to my husband about it, but I started feeling… better? I had more energy. I wasn't as annoyed at everything.

About 10 days in, he said something at breakfast.

"You seem to be in a brighter mood nowadays," with a suspicious look on his face.

"Yeah."

He didn't say anything else. Just went back to his coffee.

Then I started noticing him doing strange things — things he hadn’t done in a while. He'd ask me about my day and actually listen to my answer. He'd make the bed in the morning, which he never did. Slowly but surely, we were talking again.

Three weeks in, I woke up in the middle of the night to use the bathroom. When I came back to bed, I noticed my husband had moved. He was sleeping diagonally, with half of his body on the grounding sheet.

I didn't think much of it. 

But it kept happening. Every few nights, I'd wake up and he'd be on my side of the bed.

Then one Saturday morning, I got up early to make coffee. When I came back upstairs, he was awake, sitting on the edge of the bed.

"I need to tell you something," he said.

"What is it?"

"I think there’s something to the sheets you got."

“What do you mean?” I said.

"To be honest my back has been killing me for a while. I didn’t want to tell you because you were dealing with enough. But I could barely sleep. And then I noticed when I accidentally rolled onto your side one night, I ended up sleeping through the night. Didn’t have the aches in the morning, either."

"So you've been sleeping on the grounding sheet." I said, with the I-told-you-so look.

"Yeah. And my back is better. Not completely gone, but better than it's been in months."

He looked at me. "I guess there’s something to it. I'm sorry I gave you a hard time about buying it. I wouldn’t mind you putting it across the bed."

That was six weeks ago.

Last week, we were at dinner with our friends. 

Our friend Kate, who’s also going through menopause, was talking about her experience—night sweats, exhaustion, mood swings. All of it.

My husband said, "You should try a grounding sheet."

I was shocked. Almost spit out my wine. This man who rolled his eyes when I bought it was now recommending it to our friends.

He pulled out his phone and sent the article I'd read. Sent it to her right then and there.

"GroundingWell is the company. They let you try it for 90 days. So give it a shot."

She ordered one right then and there. Then she texted me three days later: "I haven’t slept this good in years. I love the sheets, thank your husband for me!"

But the thing that got me was Tuesday night. When he asked if I was having an affair.

After I stopped crying, he said: "The past couple of years, it felt like you were here but never actually here. And then a few weeks ago, all the sudden you came back and seemed happier. I didn't know what changed, I just knew you were different, and just thought maybe…"

“No, of course not,” I said. 

"I'm actually sleeping properly for the first time in a long time. I have the energy to do things, and everything else feels better. That’s what’s changed."

"It's not just that. You're you again. We're us again."

He was right. We'd gone from barely speaking to actually talking every day. From sleeping on opposite sides of the bed to waking up next to each other. From existing together to actually being married again.

A bedsheet didn't save my marriage. But it gave me enough sleep and enough energy to show up as myself again. And that changed everything.

Here's what I learned about why GroundingWell actually works:

It's woven with pure silver fiber that conducts the earth's electrons while you sleep. The cord plugs into your outlet's ground port—the third hole that's literally connected to the earth outside.
Those electrons help reduce inflammation and balance cortisol, which is why it helps with night sweats and sleep.

I didn't set out to fix my marriage. I just wanted to sleep.

But I learned that when you finally sleep like you were supposed to and feel like yourself again, everything else just falls in line.

If you're going through menopause and you've noticed it's affecting more than just your sleep—your relationships, your patience, your ability to show up as yourself—read this article. 

It explains everything better than I can. It’s where I got the sheet, and it’s where everything started for me.

And if your husband is skeptical, just get it anyway. Give it a few weeks. Because even he might be surprised.

Read This If You Wear Dentures 👆
My daughter helped me share this.

I never thought a pair of teeth could almost kill me.

Twenty years in the Air Force. Survived two tours. Came home in one piece. Then at 61 years old, I had a stroke sitting in my own living room watching the evening news.

My name is Ricky. I'm a retired veteran. And for the last eight years, I've worn dentures.

I thought I was doing everything right.

Soaked them every night in those blue tablets. Brushed them with paste. Rinsed them under water. Followed every instruction the dentist gave me when I first got fitted.

But nobody told me I was walking around with a ticking time bomb in my mouth.

When I retired, I didn't have dental insurance. The VA coverage I had? Bare-bones doesn't even cover it. They won't pay for cleanings. Won't pay for anything that actually matters.

By my early 50s, my teeth were shot.

I can trace it back to being a kid. My parents never taught me to brush regularly. We didn't go to the dentist—couldn't afford it. And honestly? I was drinking Mountain Dew and sweet tea like it was water. Nobody told me that stuff would rot your teeth from the inside out.

Then came the military. Twenty years of coffee, cigarettes, and grinding my teeth through stress I didn't even know I had.

By the time I realized how much it mattered, the damage was already done. Years of neglect as a kid. Years of bad habits I didn't know were bad. And then my body started breaking down on its own.

The dentist sat me down and said, "Well, you've got two options. Implants or dentures."

Then he mentioned the price. Thirty thousand dollars.

I actually laughed. Not because it was funny. Because it was so far out of reach it felt like a joke.

Implants were my dream. To eat a steak without worrying. To smile in photos without that fake look. To have teeth that didn't come out at night and sit in a cup on my bathroom sink.

But I gave this country twenty years, and the VA wouldn't even cover dentures, let alone implants.

So the choice was already made for me.

I went with dentures.

The process was hell. They pulled what was left of my real teeth. Fitted me for the plates. Sent me home with gauze stuffed in my mouth and a bottle of pain pills.

For weeks I could barely eat. My gums were swollen, bleeding. I lived on soup and mashed potatoes. 

But I told myself it was worth it. I'd have a smile again.

For a while, it was fine. I learned how to talk without them clicking. Learned how to chew carefully so they didn't slip.

Life went on.

Actually, for the first time in years, I felt like myself again.

I was eating dinner with my family. Smiling at my grandkids. Not hiding anymore.

I thought the hard part was over.

Then, about eighteen months later, I was sitting at home watching TV.

My left arm went numb.

At first, I thought I'd been sitting on it wrong. But when I tried to move it, nothing happened.

Then the left side of my face started drooping.

I tried to yell for my daughter. The words came out slurred.

I heard her scream my name. Then she was on the phone, voice shaking.

The ambulance came. At the hospital, they hooked me up to machines. A doctor kept asking me questions I couldn't answer. My left side wasn't working.

I'd had a stroke.

I survived. But when the neurologist came to talk to me after I stabilized, he asked me something I'll never forget:
"Ricky, how often do you clean your dentures?"

Every night, I told him. Soak them. Brush them. Rinse them.

He nodded slowly. Then he said, "Have you ever heard of biofilm?"

I hadn't.

He explained that dentures—even when you clean them the regular way—develop an invisible layer of bacteria called biofilm. It's a sticky, slimy coating that brushing and soaking tablets can't remove.

And that bacteria doesn't just sit there. It gets into your bloodstream. It triggers inflammation throughout your whole body. And over time, it increases your risk of stroke, heart disease, pneumonia, dementia—a whole list of things that can kill you.

He told me that studies show denture wearers are 2.3 times more likely to develop aspiration pneumonia. That bacteria from poorly cleaned dentures has been directly linked to strokes just like the one I'd had.

I felt like someone had punched me in the chest.

Here's the thing—I'd been trying to do everything else right.

I ate clean most of the time. Tried to follow that 80/20 rule, you know? Do your best, don't be perfect, but stay consistent. I took my vitamins. I took all my medications—blood thinners, cholesterol pills, the whole pharmacy bag—even though I hated it.

But I did it anyway. For my kids. For my grandkids. I wanted to be around to watch them grow up. Tried to stay active when I could. I thought I was taking care of myself.

And the whole time, the one thing I thought I had under control—my dentures—was the thing that nearly killed me.

The worst part? I couldn't even clean them properly anymore. I have arthritis in my hands. Some days I can barely grip a toothbrush. The idea of scrubbing hard enough to actually remove biofilm? Impossible.

And I was already at risk. I'm on blood thinners for God's sake. A whole cocktail of medications. My health was hanging by a thread.

So I went home from the hospital terrified. Terrified I'd have another stroke. Terrified I'd end up in a nursing home, drooling in a wheelchair, unable to speak. Terrified my grandkids would remember me that way.

I still feel betrayed. My parents never taught me how to take care of my teeth. The VA insurance wouldn't cover implants or even regular cleanings. My dentist never warned me about biofilm. And now my own body was breaking down on me.

I didn't know what to do. Honestly, I started thinking I was going to die alone. Smelling like rot. Pushed away by the people I loved most.

Then about six months ago, my daughter came over with something in her hand. A small black sphere, smooth and shiny, shaped kind of like a Magic 8 Ball.

"Dad," she said. "I need you to try this."

It was called the Denture Dome.

She told me she'd been researching denture cleaning systems for months. Trying to find something that would actually work for me—something I could use even with my arthritis, something that would kill the biofilm and keep me safe.

Now I'll be honest—I see these things on Facebook all the time. Miracle products. "As Seen on TV" garbage. I always thought they were scams.

But my daughter looked me dead in the eye and said, "Dad, this one's different. Just trust me."

She explained that the Denture Dome uses the same technology dentists use in their offices—ultrasonic cleaning combined with UV-C light sterilization.

"Dad, when you go to the dentist and they clean your dentures professionally, this is what they're using. Except instead of paying them a hundred bucks every visit, you can do it yourself at home every single night."

She said it's hospital-grade clean. The same technology they use to sterilize surgical instruments before they go into someone's body.

"This thing breaks down biofilm, Dad. It actually removes it. You don't have to scrub. And now you can thoroughly rinse them after the Clorox or harsh chemicals. 
You just put your dentures in, press one button, and it does the work for you in minutes."

I was skeptical. Hell, I was more than skeptical—I thought it was nonsense.

I'd seen a thousand of these things on Facebook. Magic pills. Miracle gadgets. All promising the world and delivering nothing but an empty wallet.

But here's the thing.

My daughter was standing there, holding that little black sphere, looking at me with hope in her eyes. Real hope. First time I'd seen that look since the stroke.

She'd spent months researching this. Months worrying about me. Months watching me fall apart.

And she was asking me to trust her.

So I said yes.

Not because I believed it would work. But because she's my daughter. And if there was even a chance—even a one percent chance—that this could help, I owed it to her to try.

Plus, she told me it was a one-time purchase. No subscription. No monthly charges. And it came with a money-back guarantee.

So I figured, what the hell. Worst case, I'm out a few bucks. Best case? Maybe I get my life back.

I said I'd give it a shot.

The first time I used it, I couldn't believe what I saw.

Gunk, food particles, film—stuff was coming off my dentures that I thought I'd been cleaning thoroughly every night.

I put my dentures in. Pressed the button and walked away for five minutes. When the cycle finished, I took them out and held them up to the bathroom light.

They looked brand new. They felt smooth. Clean. No slime. No film. No smell. Even went deep and loosened up that glue for me.

I put them in my mouth, and for the first time in months, they felt fresh.

I used it every single night after that. And within two weeks, the smell was completely gone. 

My daughter noticed. My son-in-law noticed.

But the real proof came three months later when I went back for a follow-up with my cardiologist.

He ran my bloodwork. Checked my inflammation markers. Then he looked up at me and said, "Whatever you're doing, Ricky, keep doing it. Your numbers look better than they have in years."

I told him about the Denture Dome. He actually wrote it down in his notes. Said he was going to start recommending it to his other denture patients.

But here's the thing I didn't expect.

A few weeks after I started using it, my head felt clearer. I could remember things better—names, where I put my keys, stuff I used to forget all the time. I thought maybe it was just me getting better after the stroke. But my daughter noticed it too.

"Dad, you're sharper," she said one day. "You remembered my son's friend's name. You never remember that stuff."

I don't know if it's the inflammation going down or what. But I feel more like myself. Not just physically. Mentally.

I'm telling you this because I know there are people reading this right now who are in the same spot I was.

Maybe you've had a stroke or pneumonia.

Maybe you're terrified every time you go to the doctor because you know something's wrong but nobody can tell you what.

Maybe you're just tired. Tired of the smell. Tired of scrubbing and soaking and still not feeling clean.

Maybe, like me, nobody ever taught you how to take care of your teeth when you were young. And now you're paying the price for something that wasn't even your fault.

I want you to know—there's a solution. A real one. Not some gimmick. Not some overpriced piece of junk.

I did this for my family. They're really the only thing I have left. The Denture Dome is the only thing that's ever actually removed the biofilm from my dentures. It's the only thing that's made me feel safe again. And I genuinely believe it changed my life.

Nobody warned me. Not the VA. Not my dentist. Not my doctors—until it was almost too late.

That's why I'm telling you now. I don't want another veteran, another parent, another grandparent to go through what I did.

Now I need to be clear about something: you have to order this from the official Ploise Denture Dome website. Do not buy it from Amazon. Do not buy it from Walmart or some random third-party seller. There are knockoffs out there that look similar but don't have the same ultrasonic frequency or UV-C wavelength. They don't work. And if you're trusting your health to a device like this, you need the real thing.

They've sold out three times this year already. Right now they're offering a special discount for veterans and retirees, but I don't know how long it's going to last. 
They told me supplies are limited because demand has exploded.

I grabbed the bundle—one for me, one for my wife. And honestly? I'm thinking about getting a third for our second bathroom. That's how much this thing has changed things for us.

Every night you wait, biofilm is building up again.

I spent two years living in fear. Two years convinced I was going to have another stroke. Two years avoiding my own family because I was ashamed.

I don't want that for you.

If you wear dentures, please—please—don't make the same mistake I did.

Don't assume that soaking and brushing is enough. It's not.

The bacteria is still there. The biofilm is still building up. And it's putting your health at risk every single day.

Get the Ploise Denture Dome. Use it every night. Take care of yourself the way you deserve.

And if you want that extra minty-fresh feeling? They've got tablets that work with the Dome for an even more thorough clean.

You've earned it.
